title: The Cobbler's Argot and the Charter: Pouget from the Aveyron to the Bourse du Travail
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rouergue and the Schoolboy's Paper

stops.name: Pont-de-Salars, the notary's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; date given identically by the French and English lives. Coordinate taken from the commune infobox of the French Wikipedia (44 deg 16 min 55 sec N, 2 deg 43 min 42 sec E); an earlier working figure of 44.2967, 2.7333 sat about 1.7 km northeast of the town and has been corrected.
stops.campa: In a market town of the Aveyron, above the gorges where the Viaur runs, a son is born to a notary's household on the twelfth of October, 1860. The father is dead within three years. Nothing of the Rouergue survives into the prose the son will write; the language that makes him famous is the slang of the capital's workshops, learned at a shop counter and not at a lycee desk. The town holds the birth register. It holds nothing else of him, and he does not come back to it.
suggested_refs: The civil register of Pont-de-Salars, Aveyron, for October 1860

stops.name: Salles-la-Source, the stepfather's house
stops.date_confidence: attested as to residence, reconstructed as to date: the French life places the childhood here after the mother's remarriage, without a year. The date is set to the year of the father's death purely to order the segment. Coordinate corrected to the commune point 44 deg 26 min 14 sec N, 2 deg 30 min 54 sec E; a working figure of 44.4319, 2.5614 fell in open country toward Rodez.
stops.campa: His mother remarries and the household moves to Salles-la-Source, under the limestone shelf where the water comes out of the rock in a fall the whole causse can hear. The stepfather is an employee of the public works administration, a state functionary raising a notary's son in the ordinary provincial respectability of a salaried household. The village is a dozen hamlets strung along the water, mills and a church and the Rodez road. He is twelve or thirteen when he is sent down that road to the lycee, with a boarder's trunk.
suggested_refs: The cascade and the village of Salles-la-Source, Aveyron

stops.name: Rodez, the trial of the Narbonne Communards
stops.date_confidence: the trial is attested: it opened at Rodez on 13 November 1871 and closed on the eighteenth with all forty-four civilian defendants acquitted. Pouget's presence is NOT attested. The French life says only that he was marked forever by it, with no year and no claim of attendance; an English gloss dating his witnessing of it to 1875 is chronologically impossible, since he was eleven in 1871 and not yet at the lycee. The pin is the Rodez lycee; the address of the Palais de justice is not established in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: In November 1871 the forty-four civilians taken at the Narbonne Commune are tried at Rodez, and the Rouergue watches its assizes fill with men accused of having declared a republic against the Republic. Every one of them is acquitted on the eighteenth. Pouget is eleven years old that autumn, not yet at the lycee, still up the road at Salles-la-Source. The record says he is marked forever by the trial. It does not say whether he stood in the crowd outside the courtroom or heard the whole thing secondhand.
suggested_refs: The assize records of the Aveyron for the Narbonne Commune trial, November 1871

stops.name: Rodez, Le Lycéen républicain
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1875, in both lives; no month is given for the founding of the paper or for the stepfather's death. Coordinate is the lycee of Rodez (Lycée Foch), 44.3522, 2.5655; a working figure of 44.3500, 2.5730 was about 600 m off.
stops.campa: At the lycee he founds a newspaper. Le Lycéen républicain is written by a schoolboy for schoolboys, and it is republican in the sense the word still carries in 1875, six years before the Republic is safe: hostile to the priests and the army, and ruder still about whoever holds the prefecture. In the same year his stepfather dies. The household income goes with him, and the boy who has just learned that a paper can be founded by anyone who can set type leaves the Aveyron for Paris to look for work.
suggested_refs: Le Lycéen républicain, Rodez, 1875, Pouget's first paper

segments.name: The Counter, the Black Flag, and Melun

stops.name: Paris, the counter at the Bon Marché
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the English life; no month. The quote is from a book published thirty-four years later and is placed here for what it argues, not as a statement made in 1877.
stops.campa: He is seventeen and he goes behind a counter at the Bon Marché, Boucicaut's cathedral of retail on the rue de Sèvres, where the calicot works twelve and fourteen hours for board, lodging, and the right to be dismissed at an hour's notice. Zola will publish his novel of the same trade six years later. Pouget organizes the shop instead. What he learns at that counter about the wage relation he is still setting down in pamphlets at fifty. Two years after he starts there he is helping found a union in the trade.
stops.quote: Since the day a man had the criminal ability to profit by another man's labour, since that very same day the exploited toiler has instinctively tried to give to his master less than was demanded from him.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Arturo Giovannitti (Charles H. Kerr, Chicago, 1913), Ch. 1
suggested_refs: Le Bon Marché, rue de Sèvres, Paris, the department store of the 1870s calicots
sources: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Giovannitti (1913), via theanarchistlibrary.org

stops.name: Paris, the union of shop employees
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, but the sources contradict each other on the trade: the English life calls it the first union of shop assistants in Paris, the French life dates his part in founding a Syndicat des employés du textile to the same year. The contradiction is left standing. No source names the hall. Coordinate is the corpus's standing Paris pin, used because no address is documented.
stops.campa: At nineteen he helps found a union of Paris employees, in a trade the law barely recognizes and the employers treat as domestic service. He is publishing antimilitarist tracts at the same time, which in the France of 1879 is a matter for the courts. The English and French accounts of this union do not agree with each other: one calls it the first union of shop assistants, the other a union of textile employees. Neither names the room it was founded in. Neither names anyone in it but him.
stops.quote: Between employers and workers there is never, nor ever will be made, a binding and lasting understanding, a contract in the true and loyal sense of the word.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Arturo Giovannitti (1913), Ch. 2
suggested_refs: The early Paris employees' unions of 1879, founded under the pre-1884 law

stops.name: London, the International Social Revolutionary Congress
stops.date_confidence: the congress is attested, 14 to 20 July 1881. Pouget's attendance rests on ONE source, the French life: 'En 1881, il rejoint un groupe d'anarchistes français au congrès international de Londres.' The English life does not mention the congress at all, and the article on the congress does not name him among its delegates. No source consulted names the venue; the coordinate is the corpus's standing London pin, not a located hall.
stops.campa: French anarchists cross to London in July 1881 for the International Social Revolutionary Congress, a week of delegates who agree on almost nothing except that the parliamentary road is closed. Pouget goes with them. He is twenty, four years out of the Aveyron and off a shop floor. The current he joins in that room is the one Bakunin led out of the First International, and it will still be his in 1906, when he drafts the charter that says the union answers to no party. The room itself is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The proceedings of the London International Social Revolutionary Congress, 14 to 20 July 1881
sources: mikhail_bakunin.journey.json (the anti-authoritarian minority after The Hague)

stops.name: Paris, Stéphanie Boisteux
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the English life; no month, no place within Paris, no further detail of any kind. Coordinate is the standing Paris pin.
stops.campa: In 1882 he enters the relationship that will last twenty-two years, with Stéphanie Boisteux. She is with him through the prison at Melun, the thirteen years of Le Père Peinard, the flight to London and the amnesty that brings him home. She dies in 1904, two years before the Charter of Amiens. The sources catalogue every issue number of his newspapers and every motion he drafted. About her they give a name, a year it begins, a year it ends. Where she was from, and what work she did, is in none of them.
suggested_refs: The Paris civil registers, for a partnership the biographies record only by name

stops.name: Paris, the black flag on the Esplanade des Invalides
stops.date_confidence: attested, date given identically in both lives. The claim that the anarchist black flag is flown here for the first time is the movement's own tradition, repeated by both encyclopaedias and not independently documented; treat the primacy as traditional, the march itself as attested.
stops.campa: On the ninth of March a demonstration of the unemployed forms on the esplanade of the Invalides, called against a winter with no work in it. Louise Michel is at its head, four years back from the penal colony of New Caledonia; Pouget is twenty-two and beside her. A black flag goes up here, and the movement dates its emblem to this march, on its own memory and nothing outside it. The column moves off the esplanade toward the Left Bank with the police walking behind it.
stops.quote: Instead of protesting, it were much better to resort to action. Instead of bending our heads to the orders and injunctions of the ruling classes, it would be much more effective to retaliate. Why not answer a slap with a kick?
stops.quote_source: Pouget, speech at the CGT Congress of Toulouse, 1897, quoted verbatim in Sabotage, trans. Giovannitti (1913), Ch. 1
suggested_refs: The Esplanade des Invalides, assembly point of the unemployed march of 9 March 1883

stops.name: Paris, the bakeries on the Boulevard Saint-Germain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The looting of three bakeries is attested; the route down the Boulevard Saint-Germain is inference from the endpoints, the Invalides and the Place Maubert, and is not stated as such in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The march goes down the boulevard and bread comes out of three bakers' windows and back through the crowd, which is what the charge sheet will call pillage and what the marchers call dinner. The police close from both ends. What happens between the esplanade and the Place Maubert is reconstructed afterward out of the prosecution's account and the movement's, and the two do not describe the same afternoon. No neutral statement from the boulevard is reachable.
suggested_refs: The Paris prefecture reports on the demonstration of 9 March 1883

stops.name: Paris, arrested at the Place Maubert
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the arrest at the Place Maubert and the eight-year sentence for pillage; the French life carries the sentence, the English the scene with Louise Michel. Louise Michel's own six-year term is standard in the literature on her trial and is not drawn from the Pouget articles.
stops.campa: Cornered at the Place Maubert, in the old quarter of ragpickers and cheap lodging houses, Pouget puts himself between the police and Louise Michel and is taken there. The court gives him eight years for pillage and flight. He is twenty-two when the sentence is read, and he has published one schoolboy newspaper and helped found one union. Louise Michel, tried for the same march, is given six years. The English account carries the scene with Michel, the French carries the sentence, and neither says which of the two was taken first. He will serve three of his eight.
stops.quote: Force lies at the back of every movement and every action and, of necessity, it is the culmination of these. Life is the exercise of force and, beyond force, there is only oblivion.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Direct Action (1910), English translation, theanarchistlibrary.org
suggested_refs: The Place Maubert, site of the arrest of 9 March 1883
sources: Émile Pouget, Direct Action, via theanarchistlibrary.org

stops.name: Melun, the maison centrale
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the prison; the sources disagree on the end. The French life gives the span 1883 to 1886; the English says he was released after three years following amnesty pressure and names no year. The month here is set to April 1883 only to order the segment. Coordinate is the historic maison centrale on the Île Saint-Étienne, 48.5350, 2.6622; the modern Centre pénitentiaire at Réau, 48.6009, 2.5933, is a different building and must not be substituted.
stops.campa: The maison centrale of Melun stands on the island in the Seine, an old abbey turned to the state's use, and he is held in it from 1883. Henri Rochefort campaigns in print for his release, and after roughly three years an amnesty opens the door. He is twenty-five or twenty-six when he walks out, and within two years he is editing a newspaper. The two accounts differ on how the term ended: the French gives the span as 1883 to 1886, the English says three years and pressure for amnesty, and names no year at all.
suggested_refs: The maison centrale of Melun, Île Saint-Étienne, prison of 1883 to 1886

segments.name: Le Père Peinard: the Argot Years

stops.name: Paris, editing Ça ira
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day at both ends, 27 May 1888 to 13 January 1889, in the English life. The office address is not given in any source consulted; coordinate is the standing Paris pin.
stops.campa: Out of Melun, he takes over an anarchist fortnightly called Ça ira, after the song of 1790 that promised the aristocrats would hang from the lamp posts. He edits it from the twenty-seventh of May 1888 to the thirteenth of January 1889. Where the office stood is not recorded. Eight months of it teach him that the anarchist press is written for people who already agree with it, in a French that shop assistants and dockers do not speak at home. He closes it in January. The next paper is on the street six weeks later.
suggested_refs: Ça ira, anarchist bimonthly, Paris, 1888 to 1889

stops.name: Paris, the founding of Le Père Peinard
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in both lives. The comparison with Hébert's Père Duchesne is standard in the literature on the paper and is not a claim that Pouget stated the model himself. Coordinate is the standing Paris pin; no office address is documented.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of February 1889 he launches Le Père Peinard, and invents a cobbler to write it. The Père Peinard is an old shoemaker who addresses the reader as comrade over a glass, and he speaks the argot of the Paris workshops rather than the French of the schools: the elisions, the trade slang, the obscenity, the jokes at the expense of anyone with clean hands. Hébert had done this in 1790 with the Père Duchesne; the comparison belongs to the literature, and Pouget never names the model himself. The paper is funny, and it sells.
stops.quote: Fraud, sophistication, lie, theft, fake and humbug are the warp and woof of capitalist society; to suppress them would be equal to the killing of society itself.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Arturo Giovannitti (1913), Ch. 4
suggested_refs: Le Père Peinard, Paris first series, 1889 to 1894, digitized on Gallica; the first twenty-three issues re-edited by Denis Delaplace, Classiques Garnier, 2015

stops.name: Paris, the last issue before the scoundrel laws
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the English life. The sequence of the lois scélérates of December 1893 and July 1894, and the Vaillant and Henry attacks, is the standard chronology of the period and is not drawn from the Pouget articles.
stops.campa: The bomb thrown into the Chamber of Deputies, Vaillant guillotined for it, Émile Henry's bomb in a café by the Gare Saint-Lazare: out of them come the lois scélérates, which make anarchist propaganda itself a crime and its printers accomplices. On the twenty-first of February 1894 the last Paris issue of Le Père Peinard appears. Pouget does not wait for the door. He goes south and out of France by way of Algiers, a route only the English account records; the French says merely that he was forced to emigrate to England.
suggested_refs: The lois scélérates of December 1893 and July 1894

stops.name: Algiers, the ship out
stops.date_confidence: the Algiers route rests on the English life alone; the French life says only that he was forced to emigrate to England. Month is set to March 1894 to order the segment and is not attested. Coordinate corrected to the city and old port, 36.7729, 3.0588; a working figure of 36.7867, 3.0631 lay about 1.5 km offshore in the bay.
stops.campa: He crosses to Algiers, a French port on the far side of the Mediterranean where a wanted Parisian journalist is one more passenger among soldiers, colonists and pilgrims, and takes ship from there for England. The detail is thin and stands on a single account. The police net is set at the Channel ports and the Belgian frontier, and he leaves instead through the back door of the empire. Nothing in the record says how long he waited on the quay, or under what name he sailed.
suggested_refs: The port of Algiers, 1894, and the packet routes to England

stops.name: London, the table at Defendi's delicatessen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date: the lodging with Giovanni Defendi is attested in the English life, but no month is given for his arrival, and the street of the shop is not confirmed in any source consulted. Coordinate is the corpus's standing London pin, not a located address.
stops.campa: In London he lodges at the Italian delicatessen run by Giovanni Defendi, one of the addresses where the anarchist emigration of the 1890s eats, argues, borrows money and collects its mail. Malatesta's people, Kropotkin's, the Frenchmen driven out by the scoundrel laws: London holds them all because England will not extradite for a political offence. He will spend a year of his life at this table, and the record cannot say which street it stood in.
suggested_refs: Giovanni Defendi's delicatessen, London, lodging house of the anarchist exile of the 1890s

stops.name: London, condemned in absence at the Trial of the Thirty
stops.date_confidence: the trial is attested, 6 August to 31 October 1894 at the Cour d'assises de la Seine. The outcome for Pouget is CONTRADICTED between sources and is not resolved here: the English life on Pouget says he was ultimately acquitted, while the French article on the Procès des Trente lists him explicitly as 'Émile Pouget (Condamné par contumace)', among the five accused who had gone underground. The acquittals covered the defendants who appeared in person. The stop is placed in London because that is where he was; the Palais de Justice, 48.8551, 2.3450, is where the verdict was read.
stops.campa: In Paris the state tries thirty men at once and calls it the Trial of the Thirty, mixing anarchist writers in with common thieves to prove that they are one milieu. Pouget is one of five accused who never appear. He follows it from London. The jury acquits nearly everyone standing in the dock, and here the accounts part: the English life says he too is acquitted, the French trial record lists him among those condamnés par contumace, convicted in his absence as the law required. He stays in England until the amnesty of 1895.
suggested_refs: The dossier of the Procès des Trente, Cour d'assises de la Seine, August to October 1894, Palais de Justice, Île de la Cité

stops.name: London, eight issues smuggled home
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month at both ends, September 1894 to March 1895, in the English life; the count of eight issues comes from the same source and from the French article on the paper.
stops.campa: From exile he keeps the paper alive. Eight numbers of Le Père Peinard are printed in London between September 1894 and March 1895 and carried into France disguised as ordinary pamphlets, past a police apparatus built to stop exactly this. The cobbler's voice goes on talking in Paris workshop slang out of a city where nobody speaks it. It is the smallest run of his life and the only one set in type abroad. The last London number is dated March 1895. The amnesty comes two months after it.
suggested_refs: Le Père Peinard, London series, eight issues, September 1894 to March 1895

stops.name: Paris, the amnesty and La Sociale
stops.date_confidence: attested: the amnesty is given by the French life to 1895, and the first number of La Sociale to 11 May 1895 by the English. The reading of the exile as a turn from the deed toward the union is the standard interpretation of his career and is offered as such, not as a statement of his own.
stops.campa: The amnesty of 1895 brings him home. On the eleventh of May he starts La Sociale, a paper under a new title because the old one is still legally dangerous, and takes up in Paris the argument he had been conducting from a delicatessen table. The exile has moved his target. He comes back less interested in the deed and the individual than in an organization of workers able to strike and owing nothing to any party. The old title stays in reserve for another year and a half.
suggested_refs: La Sociale, Paris, from 11 May 1895

stops.name: London, the anarchists put out of the International
stops.date_confidence: the congress is attested, London, 26 to 31 July 1896, and Pouget's attendance is attested in the English life. The VENUE is not: neither the article on the Second International nor the article on the Queen's Hall places the 1896 congress there, so the hall attribution is reconstruction and the coordinate, 51.5181, -0.1425, is the Queen's Hall, held provisionally.
stops.campa: He returns to London in July 1896 as a delegate to the Fourth Congress of the Second International, which sits for six days and settles the question Zurich had left half open. The anarchists are excluded, definitively, from the international of the socialist parties. Pouget goes home having settled it the other way round: the union, not the party, is the body that acts, and he will spend ten years building the institution that says so. Malatesta, refused his credentials, is still shouting down at the delegates from the public gallery.
suggested_refs: The proceedings of the Fourth Congress of the Second International, London, 26 to 31 July 1896

stops.name: Paris, Le Père Peinard restored
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month in the English life. The series structure is taken from the French article on the paper: Paris 1889 to 1894, London 1894 to 1895, restored title 1896 to 1899, third series January to April 1900, a single final issue in 1902. Note the contradiction in circulation: some accounts close the paper in 1900, others in 1902.
stops.campa: In October 1896 the old title comes back and the cobbler starts talking again, but the copy has changed under him. The weekly of anarchist insolence now carries strike reports, union addresses, the arithmetic of a trade's wage rates. He is arguing, issue by issue, and in the same slang, that the general strike is not a figure of speech but a thing a confederation can schedule. The paper runs in this form until 1899, returns for four months in 1900, and prints one last number in 1902. Some accounts close it in 1900 instead, and the sources consulted do not agree.
stops.quote: The worker being powerless to attack his enemy in the front, tries to do so at the side, striking him in this most vital centre: the money bag.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Arturo Giovannitti (1913), Ch. 4
suggested_refs: Le Père Peinard, restored series 1896 to 1899, and the Almanach du Père Peinard for 1894, 1896, 1897 and 1898, digitized on Gallica

stops.name: Toulouse, the congress that names sabotage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, September 1897, in both lives: the CGT congress at Toulouse adopts sabotage as a tactic after Pouget's advocacy. The brochure of that congress is titled 'Boycottage et sabottage'. An English claim of a separate 1898 pamphlet called Le Sabotage is NOT corroborated elsewhere; the book of that title is 1911, and its own opening sentence dates the word's currency to fifteen years earlier. Coordinate is the city of Toulouse; the congress hall is not named in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: At the CGT congress in Toulouse in September 1897 he puts the word sabotage into the vocabulary of the French labour movement, taking it out of the argot he has been printing for eight years. What he means is precise, and he will spend fourteen years defending the precision: not the smashing of machines for its own sake, and never harm to the consumer, but the withdrawal of the quality the employer has not paid for. The congress adopts it as a tactic. The brochure that comes out of the session is titled Boycottage et sabottage, with two t's.
stops.quote: The Congress, considering as superfluous any blame to the Government, which merely exercises its natural functions, invites the municipal workers to produce one hundred thousand francs of damage to the service in order to reward the Prefect for his veto.
stops.quote_source: Pouget's motion at the CGT Congress of Toulouse, 1897, quoted in Sabotage, trans. Giovannitti (1913), Ch. 1
suggested_refs: The brochure 'Boycottage et sabottage', CGT congress of Toulouse, September 1897

stops.name: Paris, La Voix du Peuple at the Bourse du Travail
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in both lives: the first number of La Voix du Peuple, 1 December 1900, under Pouget's editorship. Coordinate corrected to the Bourse du travail de Paris, 3 rue du Château d'Eau, 48.8689, 2.3620; a working figure of 48.8703, 2.3605 sat on the wrong side of the block.
stops.campa: On the first of December 1900 the first number of La Voix du Peuple appears, and the confederation has a paper of its own with Pouget in the editor's chair. He works out of the Bourse du Travail on the rue du Château d'Eau, the labour exchange the municipality built and the unions occupied, where a man out of work can find a job, a meeting, a lawyer and a printing press in the same building. He will edit it for eight years, through every strike the CGT calls.
stops.quote: Sabotage must be directed against the boss either by reducing the output or by deteriorating and making unusable the product or by disabling and paralysing the instruments of production, but the consumer, we repeat, must never suffer by this war waged exclusively against the exploiter.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Arturo Giovannitti (1913), Ch. 4
suggested_refs: La Voix du Peuple, organ of the CGT, from 1 December 1900; the Bourse du travail, 3 rue du Château d'Eau, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the federations section
stops.date_confidence: the sources disagree and the disagreement is left standing: the French life makes him assistant secretary of the CGT's federations section from 1901, the English makes him vice-secretary heading that section from the 1902 merger with the Fédération des Bourses du Travail. The date here takes the earlier of the two only to order the segment. The merger of 1902 itself is not in dispute.
stops.campa: He is taken into the confederation's leadership and given the federations section: the trade federations, as against the bourses, the two halves of French unionism that merge in 1902 into one body. The accounts differ on his title and his year, assistant secretary from 1901 in the French, vice-secretary from 1902 in the English. The function is not in dispute. For the years the revolutionary current runs strongest inside the CGT, he drafts its texts and counts its votes.
stops.quote: Capital and labour are two worlds that violently clash together!
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Arturo Giovannitti (1913), Ch. 2
suggested_refs: The CGT's federations section, 1901 to 1908, and the 1902 merger with the Fédération des Bourses du Travail

stops.name: Paris, the death of Stéphanie Boisteux
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1904, in the English life. Neither the day, the month, the place, nor the cause is given anywhere consulted; the coordinate is the standing Paris pin and is a placeholder, not a location of death.
stops.campa: Stéphanie Boisteux dies in 1904, after twenty-two years together. The sources do not give the day, the place, or the cause of her death. He is forty-three, editor of the confederation's paper and assistant secretary of its federations, and the record of the movement he is building has room for every motion he drafted that year and none for this. Whether he put the paper down that week, whether anyone at the Bourse du Travail knew, is not recorded anywhere consulted.
suggested_refs: The Paris death registers for 1904

stops.name: Amiens, the drafting of the Charter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the commemorative plaque quoted by the French article reads 'adoption de la charte d'Amiens, le 13 octobre 1906', and the same article confirms the drafting verbatim, 'cette motion, rédigée par Victor Griffuelhes et Émile Pouget'. The vote is recorded as 830 of 839. CAVEAT on the venue: the sources attest the PLAQUE at the École Albert Roze, rue Rigollot, not that the congress sat there. Coordinate is rue Rigollot, 49.8870, 2.3100; a working figure of 49.8968, 2.2993 lay 1.4 km away in the city centre.
stops.campa: At the ninth congress of the CGT, on the thirteenth of October 1906, the motion drafted by Victor Griffuelhes and Émile Pouget carries by eight hundred and thirty votes out of eight hundred and thirty-nine. The Charter of Amiens states that the union suffices: it pursues wages and hours today and prepares the whole expropriation tomorrow, and it recognizes no party, no church and no sect above itself. It settles, in a French union hall, the quarrel that broke the First International when Marx had Bakunin expelled at The Hague thirty-four years before.
stops.quote: Direct Action is the symbol of revolutionary unionism in action.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Direct Action (1910), English translation, theanarchistlibrary.org
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque of the Charte d'Amiens, rue Rigollot, Amiens; the text of the motion of 13 October 1906

stops.name: Vigneux-sur-Seine, the gendarmes fire into the quarry strike
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the sand-quarry strike began at Draveil on 2 May 1908, and on 2 June gendarmes fired at Vigneux, killing Pierre Le Foll, aged 48, and Émile Giobellina, aged 17, and wounding about ten. An English gloss dating the deaths to May and treating May as the END of the strikes is wrong on both counts; the strike ran to the first week of August.
stops.campa: The sand quarries along the Seine at Draveil and Vigneux come out on strike on the second of May 1908, for a wage the pit owners will not pay. La Voix du Peuple carries the strike week by week while the Paris press reports it as a question of public order. The strike is a month old when the gendarmes fire into the strikers at Vigneux, on the second of June. Pierre Le Foll, forty-eight years old, and Émile Giobellina, seventeen, are killed. About ten men are wounded.
stops.quote: The people, sentimental and soft-hearted, display nothing of the endemic violence that characterises the ruling classes, and which is the mortar holding their rule together.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Direct Action (1910), English translation, theanarchistlibrary.org
suggested_refs: The sand quarries of Draveil and Vigneux-sur-Seine, on strike from 2 May 1908

stops.name: Villeneuve-Saint-Georges, the thirtieth of July
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: four strikers killed and more than two hundred wounded at Vigneux and Villeneuve-Saint-Georges on 30 July 1908; work resumed between 4 and 8 August. Clemenceau's role as président du conseil and minister of the interior is standard for the period and not drawn from the Pouget articles.
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of July the cavalry go into the crowd at Villeneuve-Saint-Georges. Four strikers are killed and more than two hundred are wounded, and the minister who has sent them is Georges Clemenceau, who entered politics on the far left of the Republic and is now called the first cop of France in every union hall in the country. The strike breaks in the first week of August. The men go back down into the pits between the fourth and the eighth, on the owners' terms.
suggested_refs: The dead of Villeneuve-Saint-Georges and Vigneux, 30 July 1908

stops.name: Paris, the arrest of the thirty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested to the days, 30 and 31 July 1908, in the French article on the strikes: thirty-one CGT leaders charged, among them Griffuelhes the secretary-general, Pouget as editor of La Voix du Peuple, Yvetot, Dret, and Monatte, who got out to Switzerland. An English gloss dating the arrests to a vaguer 1908 or to August is corrected here. No source names the place of Pouget's arrest; coordinate is the standing Paris pin.
stops.campa: On the thirtieth and thirty-first of July, with the dead not yet buried, the government arrests the confederation's leadership. Thirty-one men are charged: Victor Griffuelhes the secretary-general, Georges Yvetot, Pouget as editor of La Voix du Peuple. Pierre Monatte gets across the Swiss border. Whatever the charge sheet says, the effect is that the CGT's entire executive is in cells while its strike collapses in the pits. No source consulted says where Pouget was taken, or by whom.
suggested_refs: The July 1908 charge sheet against the thirty-one leaders of the CGT

stops.name: Paris, the non-lieu
stops.date_confidence: the release is attested to 30 October 1908, when a non-lieu was pronounced for all thirty-one. The English life's February 1909 release date is CONTRADICTED and appears to conflate two events: the Chamber's amnesty covering 2 May 1908 to 15 January 1909 was voted on 11 February 1909, by 451 to 5, three months after he was already out. The PRISON is not named in any source consulted; the coordinate is approximate for Paris and marks no identified building.
stops.campa: He is held from the end of July to the thirtieth of October 1908, when a non-lieu is pronounced and the case against all thirty-one is dropped without ever reaching a trial. Which Paris prison held him is not named in any reachable source. The English account puts his release in February 1909, which is the date of something else: on the eleventh of February the Chamber votes an amnesty for the offences of the strike months, four hundred and fifty-one to five. By then he has been out for three months.
suggested_refs: The non-lieu of 30 October 1908 and the amnesty vote of 11 February 1909

stops.name: Paris, La Révolution
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month at both ends, February to March 1909, in the English life. Note that the same source ties the launch to his release; the release was four months earlier, and the two events are separate. The reasons for the failure are inference from the run length and are not stated in any source consulted.
stops.campa: In February 1909 he puts everything into a daily called La Révolution, meant to carry revolutionary syndicalism into the ordinary news of an ordinary morning. It folds in March. No source consulted gives a reason; a daily costs what a weekly does not, and the confederation is broke after the summer of the quarries. It is the first outright failure of his working life as a publisher. How many numbers it managed in those weeks is not stated anywhere reachable, and no copy of it was read. He is forty-eight.
suggested_refs: La Révolution, Paris, February to March 1909

stops.name: Paris, columnist for La Guerre sociale
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1909, in the English life; no month, and the month here orders the segment only. Hervé's later trajectory to the far right and to support for Pétain is standard biography for him and is not drawn from the Pouget articles. Coordinate is the standing Paris pin; the paper's office address is not documented in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: He goes to work as a columnist on Gustave Hervé's La Guerre sociale, the most violently antimilitarist paper in France, whose editor is at this point telling conscripts to plant the tricolour in a dungheap. Hervé will end his life on the far right, campaigning for Pétain. Pouget is writing for other men's papers now, on other men's subjects, for the first time since he came out of Melun. The office he writes from is not documented anywhere consulted. He is forty-nine years old, and he has no paper of his own.
suggested_refs: La Guerre sociale, Gustave Hervé's antimilitarist weekly, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the novel written with Pataud
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1909, in the English life: Comment nous ferons la révolution, co-written with Émile Pataud. Pataud's position in the electricians' union is standard biography for him. The account of the book's reception in union halls is characterization of the genre, not a documented circulation figure.
stops.campa: With Émile Pataud, of the electricians' union, the man who can put Paris in the dark by telephone, he writes a novel. Comment nous ferons la révolution imagines the general strike carried all the way through: the unions take the works, the state falls without a battle, and a federated France runs itself out of the bourses du travail. It is fiction of the movement, written to be read aloud. The argument is that the thing can be pictured hour by hour, and the book spends its whole length picturing it. No source consulted gives what it sold or who read it.
suggested_refs: Émile Pataud and Émile Pouget, Comment nous ferons la révolution (1909)

stops.name: Paris, L'Action directe
stops.date_confidence: the pamphlet is dated 1910 by the English translation consulted at theanarchistlibrary.org, which gives neither translator nor edition; the French bibliography also carries La Confédération générale du travail to 1910, in Marcel Rivière's Bibliothèque du mouvement prolétarien. Month is not attested and orders the segment only. The quote is given in the source's own wording, opening conjunction and two-dot ellipsis included.
stops.campa: He writes the pamphlet that names the method. Direct action means that the workers act for themselves, through their own organization, without deputies, without intermediaries and without asking the state to legislate what they are able to take: the strike, the boycott, the union label, the go-slow, sabotage. Parliament enters the text only as the thing being gone around. In the same year he publishes La Confédération générale du travail, the confederation explained to the men inside it.
stops.quote: Because action is the salt of life ... Or, to put it more plainly and simply, it is life itself! To live is to act .. To act is to be alive!
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Direct Action (1910), English translation, theanarchistlibrary.org
suggested_refs: Émile Pouget, L'Action directe (1910), reissued by Le Flibustier; La Confédération générale du travail (1910), Bibliothèque du mouvement prolétarien
sources: Émile Pouget, Direct Action, via theanarchistlibrary.org

stops.name: Paris, Le Sabotage set down as a book
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1911, by the French article on sabotage; the book opens by dating the word's currency to some fifteen years earlier, which fits 1911 and not the 1898 sometimes given. The series is the Bibliothèque du mouvement prolétarien, Marcel Rivière's imprint, NOT the CGT's own press as one account states. The Giovannitti translation, Charles H. Kerr, Chicago, 1913, is a standard bibliographic record.
stops.campa: Fourteen years after Toulouse he sets the whole theory down as a book, in the Bibliothèque du mouvement prolétarien, the series Marcel Rivière prints for the syndicalists. Sabotage is the weapon of the side that cannot meet the other in the open field: cut the output, spoil the product, stop the machine, and never, on any account, injure the person who buys the thing. Two years later an Italian American poet, Arturo Giovannitti, translates it in Chicago for Charles H. Kerr, and the word goes into the working vocabulary of the Industrial Workers of the World.
stops.quote: Sabotage as a form of revolt is as old as human exploitation.
stops.quote_source: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Arturo Giovannitti (Charles H. Kerr, Chicago, 1913), Ch. 1
suggested_refs: Émile Pouget, Le Sabotage (1911), Bibliothèque du mouvement prolétarien; the Giovannitti translation, Charles H. Kerr, Chicago, 1913; the Mille et une nuits reissue, 2004
sources: Émile Pouget, Sabotage, trans. Giovannitti (1913), via theanarchistlibrary.org

segments.name: The War, the Marriage, and the Silence

stops.name: Paris, stories for L'Humanité
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1913, in the English life: stories published in Jaurès's L'Humanité. Coordinate corrected to the paper's offices at 142 rue Montmartre, 48.8689, 2.3434; a working figure of 48.8674, 2.3494 landed near the rue Réaumur. The reading of the reformist turn inside the CGT after 1909 is standard historiography and is not a claim from the Pouget articles.
stops.campa: He writes stories for L'Humanité, the paper Jean Jaurès founded, at 142 rue Montmartre. It is not where the man who drafted the Charter of Amiens would be expected to publish: L'Humanité is the socialist party's paper, and the charter exists to say that the union owes the party nothing. He is fifty-three. The syndicalist current he led has been losing ground inside the confederation since 1909 and the reformists hold it now. He publishes there anyway.
suggested_refs: The offices of L'Humanité, 142 rue Montmartre, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the position of national defence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, August 1914, in the English life, which calls the alignment unexpected. The assassination of Jaurès on 31 July 1914 and the CGT's failure to call the promised general strike are standard chronology for the period. No text of Pouget's own explaining the turn is cited in any source consulted, and none was located.
stops.campa: Jaurès is shot dead in a café off the rue Montmartre on the thirty-first of July 1914, and the war comes four days later. The CGT, which had promised a general strike against mobilization, does not call one. Pouget, who has spent thirty years arguing that the worker has no country and that the army is the employer's instrument, takes the position of national defence against Germany. The English life calls the turn unexpected and offers nothing further. No text of Pouget's own explaining it is cited in any source consulted, and none was located.
suggested_refs: The Union sacrée of August 1914 and the CGT's abandoned general strike

stops.name: Paris, the marriage at the mairie of the eighteenth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the French life, verbatim: 'Il se marie, le 17 avril 1915 dans le 18e arrondissement de Paris, avec Augustine Caroline Jamaux.' The English life does not mention the marriage at all and refers only to his wife. Coordinate is the Mairie du 18e, place Jules Joffrin, 48.8922, 2.3441.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of April 1915, in the eighteenth arrondissement, in the second year of the war, Émile Pouget marries Augustine Caroline Jamaux. He is fifty-four. The English account of his life does not mention the marriage at all and speaks only of his wife; the French gives the day, the arrondissement and her name in full, and nothing further about her exists in the reachable record. He will live with her sixteen years, almost all of them out of public life.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of the Mairie du 18e arrondissement, Paris, 17 April 1915

stops.name: Paris, Vieille Alsace
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1915, in the English life: a daily serial titled Vieille Alsace, written for L'Humanité. No month or run length is given anywhere consulted; the month here orders the segment only. Coordinate is the paper's offices at 142 rue Montmartre.
stops.campa: Through 1915 he writes a daily serial for L'Humanité called Vieille Alsace, old Alsace, about the province France lost in 1871 and is now spending a generation of men to win back. It is patriotic feuilleton, an old province and its costumes and its churches, printed under the name of the man who invented the Père Peinard and taught a generation of readers to laugh at the flag. It runs daily, which nothing of his has done since La Révolution folded inside a month. It is the last regular writing work of his life.
suggested_refs: Vieille Alsace, daily serial, L'Humanité, 1915

stops.name: Palaiseau, the catalogues at Lozère
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 1920 in the English life: by this point he has ceased political activism, lives south of Paris and compiles catalogues of artists' works. Coordinate corrected to the Lozère quarter of Palaiseau, 48.7046, 2.2066, with Lozère station at 48.7060, 2.2118; working figures of 48.7053, 2.2394 and 48.7167, 2.2455 both sit well east of Lozère.
stops.campa: By 1920 he has stopped. He lives at Lozère, a quarter of Palaiseau on the southern edge of Paris where the line runs up the Yvette valley, and he earns his living compiling catalogues of artists' works: titles, dimensions, provenance, prices. He is sixty when he starts, and the work is exact and unhurried and nobody is waiting on it. Who paid him for the catalogues is not named. Whether anyone from the confederation came out on the train to see him is not recorded in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: The Lozère quarter of Palaiseau and its station on the Sceaux line

stops.name: Palaiseau, death at Lozère
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in both lives: died 21 July 1931 at Lozère, in Palaiseau, then in Seine-et-Oise, aged seventy. The absence of any monument, statue or plaque is an absence noted across both encyclopaedia entries, not a documented negative.
stops.campa: He dies at Lozère on the twenty-first of July 1931, seventy years old. Palaiseau is then in Seine-et-Oise, open country with a station on the line into the city, and he has been living in it for something over a decade. No monument, no statue and no plaque to him is recorded in Palaiseau or in Paris in any source consulted. He had been out of the movement's public life for eleven years, and five years before his death the confederation he built split into two rival bodies, neither of them his.
suggested_refs: The death register of Palaiseau, Seine-et-Oise, July 1931

stops.name: Palaiseau, the grave
stops.date_confidence: the burial at the cemetery of Palaiseau and the three named mourners are attested in the French life; the day of the burial is not given and is set here to the day after the death, to order the segment. Coordinate is the only cemetery within the commune of Palaiseau in OpenStreetMap, way 25413308, centroid 48.7103, 2.2360; a working figure of 48.7126, 2.2453 was about 700 m off.
stops.campa: He is buried in the cemetery of Palaiseau. Pierre Monatte, who got over the Swiss border in 1908 while Pouget went into a cell, stands at the grave; so does Maurice Chambelland, Monatte's man on La Révolution prolétarienne; so does Daniel Guérin, a young man who will spend the next fifty years writing the history of this movement. What has become of the grave since, whether it still stands, whether anyone tends it, is not recorded in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: The cemetery of Palaiseau, Essonne; the reissues that carry his texts instead of stone: Mille et une nuits (2004), Les Nuits rouges (2006), Classiques Garnier (2015)
